title: HE CAME IN PEACE. THEY CARRIED HIM OUT DEAD. AND THE MAN WHO KILLED HIM KEPT HIS POWER.
paragraphs: HE CAME IN PEACE. THEY CARRIED HIM OUT DEAD. AND THE MAN WHO KILLED HIM KEPT HIS POWER.
The chilling betrayal of Abner, the blood on Joab's hands, and the terrifying truth about what happens when people mistake God's patience for His approval. — 2 Samuel 3:26–39; 1 Kings 2:5–6
He survived the battlefield.
He survived the collapse of a kingdom.
He survived years of political conflict, shifting loyalties, and men who would have gladly watched him die.
Then he walked into a place where he believed he was safe.
And that was where they killed him.
Not in the heat of battle.
Not while defending himself against an advancing army.
Not with a sword already drawn.
He was taken aside as though someone wanted to speak privately.
And a blade entered his body.
His name was Abner.
The man who killed him was Joab.
And the most frightening part of this account is that Joab did not immediately lose his position, his influence, or his access to power.
He continued serving as a commander.
He continued standing near the throne.
He continued living as though the blood he had spilled could somehow disappear beneath the weight of his accomplishments.
But God had not forgotten.
Before we go any further, we need to confront something that has been circulating in dramatic retellings of this story.
Some versions claim that a woman was commanded to marry the man who had murdered her husband, and that she courageously refused.
It is a shocking image.
It makes you angry before you even finish reading it.
But Scripture does not record that happening in the account of Joab and Abner.
The Bible does not identify Abner's widow, describe Joab demanding her hand, or record a woman refusing such a marriage.
And if we truly love the Word of God, we cannot manufacture an injustice to make a biblical account more compelling.
The truth is already powerful.
The real betrayal is already horrifying.
And what God reveals through it is far more important than any invented scandal.
Because sometimes the most dangerous person in the room is not the one openly carrying a weapon.
Sometimes it is the one smiling while concealing a wound that has never healed.
To understand what happened, we must return to a divided Israel.
King Saul was dead.
David had been anointed king, but the entire nation had not yet united under his rule.
Abner, the commander of Saul's army, had supported Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, while David ruled over Judah.
The conflict between the two royal houses continued.
And then something changed.
Abner decided to transfer his allegiance to David.
In 2 Samuel 3, Abner began working toward bringing Israel under David's kingship.
This was no ordinary political conversation.
It represented the possibility of ending a bitter division that had already cost lives.
David received Abner and the men accompanying him.
A feast was held.
An agreement was discussed.
And David sent Abner away in peace.
That final detail matters.
In the Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:21, the expression is:
וַיְשַׁלַּח דָּוִד אֶת־אַבְנֵר וַיֵּלֶךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם
Vayeshalach David et-Avner, vayelekh beshalom.
The sense is:
“David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.”
The Hebrew word shalom (שָׁלוֹם) carries the sense of peace, well-being, and wholeness.
Abner was not being sent away as a condemned prisoner.
He was leaving under peaceful terms.
He had every reason to believe the conversation was over.
But someone else was not ready for peace.
Joab had returned from a military expedition.
When he learned that Abner had visited David and departed safely, he became furious.
Joab accused Abner of deception.
He warned David that Abner had come to spy on him.
But beneath the political accusations was another story.
A family wound.
A dead brother.
A debt Joab believed had not been paid.
Earlier, during the conflict between David's forces and the forces loyal to Saul's house, Abner had killed Joab's brother Asahel.
Yet the circumstances were profoundly different.
According to 2 Samuel 2:18–23, Asahel relentlessly pursued Abner during battle.
Abner repeatedly warned him to turn aside.
Asahel refused.
Abner finally struck him with the butt end of his spear, killing him.
It was tragic.
It devastated Joab's family.
But Scripture presents Asahel's death within the circumstances of armed conflict, not as the same kind of deliberate, deceptive killing that Joab would later commit.
Joab, however, was not willing to leave the matter there.
He wanted blood.
And when David chose peace with Abner, Joab chose revenge.
Without David's knowledge, Joab sent messengers after Abner.
They brought him back from the well of Sirah.
Then, at Hebron, Joab drew Abner aside near the city gate.
The Bible describes the encounter with a chilling detail.
Joab approached as though he intended to speak with Abner privately.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 3:27 includes the phrase:
לְדַבֵּר אִתּוֹ בַּשֶּׁלִי
Ledabber itto basheli.
The expression conveys speaking with him privately or quietly.
It describes the appearance of a private conversation, not an open battlefield confrontation.
And that is what makes the next moment so disturbing.
Joab struck Abner in the abdomen.
Abner died.
The man who had just left David in peace was now lying dead because another man had decided that revenge mattered more than reconciliation.
Imagine the sudden realization.
A familiar face.
A quiet conversation.
A moment when no attack was expected.
And then the unbearable discovery that the person standing close enough to speak was standing close enough to kill.
There was no opportunity for Abner to negotiate.
No opportunity to defend his decision to make peace.
No opportunity to explain himself to the man whose brother he had killed in battle.
The account gives us no final speech from Abner.
Only the devastating fact of his death.
And Joab walked away having done what he intended to do.
But the blood did not become innocent simply because Joab believed his anger was justified.
That is where this ancient story begins reaching into our lives.
Because most of us will never stand at the gate of Hebron holding a weapon.
But we know what it means to be wounded.
We know what it means to replay an offense until the memory becomes almost unbearable.
We know what it means to imagine the conversation we wish we could have.
The apology we never received.
The consequences we wish someone would suffer.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we begin treating our pain as permission.
Permission to humiliate.
Permission to retaliate.
Permission to destroy a reputation.
Permission to withhold mercy.
Permission to become cruel because someone else was cruel first.
But being wounded does not make every response righteous.
And being right about the existence of an injury does not make every act of revenge just.
Joab had truly lost his brother.
His grief was not imaginary.
But his grief did not give him authority to murder a man who had been received and dismissed in peace.
A real wound can explain your anger without excusing what your anger makes you do.
Read that again.
Because someone reading this may have spent years waiting for another person to suffer enough to make the past feel fair.
Someone may be carrying resentment so deeply that it has become part of their identity.
Someone may have confused refusing to forgive with refusing to let evil win.
Yet Scripture does not teach that forgiveness means calling evil good.
It does not teach that reconciliation must happen without repentance, accountability, or safety.
And it certainly does not teach that victims must remain in harmful situations.
What it teaches is that personal vengeance must not become our god.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” (KJV)
That is not permission for evil to escape justice.
It is a warning that we must not appoint ourselves the final judges of another person's life.
Joab crossed that line.
And then came the consequences.
When David heard what had happened, he publicly declared that he and his kingdom were innocent of Abner's blood.
He pronounced judgment upon Joab's house.
He ordered mourning.
He followed Abner's funeral procession.
He wept at Abner's grave.
And he lamented that Abner had died a shameful death, even though Abner had not been bound like a criminal.
David's grief was visible.
His condemnation was public.
The people understood that Abner's death had not been ordered by the king.
But there is another uncomfortable detail.
Joab was not immediately executed.
David acknowledged that although he was anointed king, he was still weak in relation to the sons of Zeruiah, Joab and his brother Abishai.
He ended his lament in 2 Samuel 3:39 by appealing to God to repay the evildoer according to his wickedness.
And here we encounter one of the most unsettling realities in Scripture.
A man can be publicly condemned for evil and still remain influential.
A person can be guilty and still retain a title.
Someone can do terrible things and continue receiving honor from people who do not know, do not care, or feel powerless to intervene.
That does not mean God has approved.
It means earthly consequences do not always arrive as quickly as we expect.
And David's own failure to remove Joab immediately should not be romanticized as an ideal example of justice.
The narrative shows the difficulty and weakness surrounding David's position.
It does not tell us that powerful men should be allowed to escape accountability.
In fact, the story becomes darker.
Years later, Joab killed another military commander, Amasa.
Second Samuel 20:9–10 describes Joab greeting Amasa with apparent friendliness, taking hold of his beard as though to kiss him, and then striking him with a sword.
Again, familiarity concealed violence.
Again, a gesture associated with trust became the setting for betrayal.
Again, Joab's weapon did what his words did not announce.
This was not simply one terrible moment from a grieving brother.
It became a recognizable pattern.
And by the time David approached death, he had not forgotten.
In 1 Kings 2:5, David reminded Solomon what Joab had done to Abner and Amasa.
The Hebrew description includes:
דְּמֵי־מִלְחָמָה בְּשָׁלֹם
Demei-milchamah beshalom.
Literally, the expression conveys “blood of war in peace.”
What a devastating indictment.
Blood that belonged to the violence of war had been brought into the conditions of peace.
Joab had treated peace as though it were merely another opportunity to attack.
And David told Solomon not to allow Joab's guilt to go unanswered.
The judgment was eventually carried out in 1 Kings 2:28–34 after Joab supported Adonijah's unsuccessful claim to the throne and fled to the tabernacle, taking hold of the horns of the altar.
Joab sought refuge at a sacred place.
But the altar was not a magical escape from accountability for deliberate murder.
Exodus 21:14 had already established that someone who intentionally and treacherously killed another person could not use God's altar as protection from judgment.
Solomon ordered Joab's execution.
Benaiah carried it out.
And the bloodshed that had followed Joab through years of influence finally met its earthly consequence.
The delay had been long.
But the story was not forgotten.
Still, we must be careful here.
We cannot promise that every murderer will be punished in this life.
We cannot tell every betrayed person that justice will arrive before they die.
We cannot look at someone's suffering and claim to know exactly what God is doing behind it.
The Bible itself contains the cries of righteous people who cannot understand why the wicked prosper.
But Scripture does assure us that God is just, that evil matters, and that no human being escapes His ultimate judgment.
And this is where the story becomes even more personal.
Because it is easy to read about Joab and say, “What a wicked man.”
It is harder to ask whether there are smaller forms of his spirit of retaliation living inside our own hearts.
Not because ordinary resentment is morally identical to murder.
It is not.
But because Jesus teaches us to examine the roots of sin, not merely its most visible consequences.
In Matthew 5:21–22, Jesus moves beyond the prohibition against murder to confront sinful anger and contempt.
He does not erase the distinction between anger and killing.
He exposes the heart from which destructive actions can grow.
And suddenly, this is no longer only a story about Joab.
It is about the person who cannot stop rehearsing revenge.
The Christian who sings about grace but refuses to extend mercy.
The believer who wants God to forgive their own sins while demanding that everyone else's failures define them forever.
The wounded soul who has allowed bitterness to occupy a room that once belonged to peace.
Perhaps you have been betrayed.
Perhaps someone used your trust against you.
Perhaps someone smiled while quietly destroying something precious to you.
And perhaps you are reading this with tears you have never allowed anyone else to see.
Hear this carefully.
Jesus does not require you to pretend that what happened was acceptable.
He does not ask you to deny the wound.
He does not command you to trust someone who remains dangerous.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for truth, boundaries, protection, or appropriate accountability.
But Christ does call you to surrender the throne of vengeance.
Because revenge cannot resurrect what you lost.
And hatred cannot become the savior of a wounded heart.
Only Jesus can save.
There is something else in this account that should make every one of us tremble.
Joab remained close to sacred things.
He served the king whom God had chosen.
He participated in the history of God's covenant people.
He occupied a position of remarkable importance.
Yet proximity to God's purposes did not make his private violence righteous.
And proximity to religious activity does not automatically mean a person's heart belongs to Christ.
You can know the language of faith and still resist the Lord of faith.
You can defend a ministry and still refuse repentance.
You can speak passionately about righteousness while hiding the sins you do not want anyone to confront.
You can be useful in the eyes of people and desperately in need of mercy before God.
That is why the Gospel does not begin by telling us how impressive we are.
It tells us the truth about our sin.
Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
But the Gospel does not leave us standing beneath condemnation without hope.
Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners, through Christ's death for us.
And here is the astonishing difference between the violence of Joab and the victory of Jesus.
Joab used betrayal to take another man's life.
Jesus was betrayed and willingly gave His own life for sinners.
Joab's violence exposed the ugliness of human vengeance.
Christ's cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the extraordinary mercy of God.
Joab sought to settle a debt through another man's blood.
Jesus shed His own blood to accomplish the redemption that no sinner could ever earn.
The comparison is not that Abner's death and Christ's death were the same.
They were not.
Abner was a political and military leader killed through treachery.
Jesus is the sinless Son of God who gave Himself as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
And Jesus did not merely become another victim of human evil.
He willingly laid down His life, according to John 10:17–18, and rose again in victory over death.
The cross is not God's approval of injustice.
It is the place where divine justice and saving mercy meet through the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
And that is why even the person who recognizes something of Joab's darkness within themselves is not beyond the call to repentance.
Perhaps you have never killed anyone.
But you have wounded people with your words.
Perhaps you have never drawn a sword.
But you have destroyed trust.
Perhaps you have never betrayed someone at a city gate.
But you have smiled while concealing resentment.
Or perhaps you are the one who has been hurt, and the burden you are carrying is slowly exhausting your soul.
The invitation of Jesus reaches both the guilty who need forgiveness and the wounded who need healing.
Not through denial.
Not through excuses.
Not through religious performance.
Through repentance and faith in Him.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
That promise does not make sin insignificant.
It reveals how sufficient Christ's sacrifice truly is.
And if the Holy Spirit is exposing something hidden in your heart as you read this, do not rush past that conviction.
Do not turn it into another moment of religious emotion that disappears as soon as you close your phone.
Bring it before Jesus.
Name the bitterness.
Confess the cruelty.
Admit the resentment.
Ask Him to teach you how to forgive without abandoning wisdom, how to seek justice without becoming consumed by revenge, and how to walk in truth without surrendering to hatred.
Maybe your prayer is only a whisper.

“Lord Jesus, I have been carrying this for too long. I don't know how to release it. But I don't want my pain to become my master. Forgive my sins. Heal what has been wounded. Teach me to trust You with justice. Change my heart.”
You do not need eloquent words to come to Christ.
You need a heart willing to come honestly.
And if that prayer reflects what you are going through, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
Not because a comment earns God's favor.
Not because public confession is required for forgiveness.
But because sometimes a simple, honest response can become the beginning of a conversation, a request for prayer, or an encouragement to another person who thought they were suffering alone.
If you are not ready to share your struggle publicly, that is okay. Bring it privately to the Lord, and consider speaking with a trustworthy Christian who can walk beside you.
Someone may need to know that healing is possible without pretending the past never happened.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is still possible after serious failure.
Someone may need to remember that the Gospel is not only for people who appear to have their lives together.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn Scripture into sensational entertainment.
Not to manufacture scandals the Bible never recorded.
Not to replace sound biblical teaching with emotional manipulation.
But to bring people back to the living Word of God, where truth confronts us, grace humbles us, and Jesus Christ transforms us.
Every article, every devotional, every Scripture reflection, and every resource is part of that mission.
And if this message has helped you see God's Word more clearly, there are meaningful ways you can help it reach someone else.
Not simply because you liked it, but because someone in your circle may be quietly battling the same bitterness, betrayal, or spiritual exhaustion described here.

And invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown weary, the person who has drifted from church, and even the skeptic who has questions about Christianity to explore these messages for themselves.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond momentary inspiration into consistent study, prayer, spiritual maturity, and a closer walk with the Lord.
And if you believe this work is worth sustaining, I want to invite you into a deeper level of partnership.
For those who choose to give regularly as an expression of Christian generosity, that support can be part of their personal stewardship and offering to the Lord.
Christians may honor the Lord through faithful giving to their local church, caring for those in need, supporting trustworthy Gospel ministries, and serving others with love.
Scripture reminds us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure or compulsion.
We want your partnership to come from conviction, gratitude, and genuine belief in this mission.
These items can be reminders of faith, encouragement in daily life, or meaningful gifts for others.
It is the opportunity to help make ongoing biblical encouragement and discipleship available to more people.
His grace is not merchandise.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
That truth is too precious to compromise.
Because one day, everything we have built will be tested against what is eternally true.
The influence.
The reputation.
The public approval.
The applause.
Even the religious activities we were proud of.
None of those things can cleanse a guilty conscience.
None can reconcile a sinner to God.
Only Christ can.
And that brings us back to Joab.
A man who possessed enormous power but could not make his violence righteous.
A man who stood close to a king but could not escape accountability forever.
A man whose actions remind us that success is not proof of innocence, delay is not proof of divine approval, and the appearance of peace is not always the presence of righteousness.
But we do not have to end this story staring only at Joab's darkness.
We can look toward the greater King.
The King who did not come to establish His kingdom through treacherous murder.
The King who was betrayed, condemned, crucified, and raised from the dead.
The King who offers forgiveness to repentant sinners and calls His people to walk in truth, mercy, justice, and holiness.
His name is Jesus.
And no matter whether you recognize yourself today in the wounded, the angry, the ashamed, or the spiritually exhausted, His invitation remains.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Him.
Let His truth expose what needs to change.
Let His grace meet what you cannot repair.
And let His Spirit begin transforming what bitterness has tried to claim.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply that Joab carried violence in his heart.
It is that a human heart can become so accustomed to its own darkness that it stops recognizing the need for light.
Do not let that happen to yours.
The wound you refuse to surrender may become the weapon you never intended to carry.
